title: Democrats Pass 250 House Seats, Biggest Majority Since 2008 as Count Continues
excerpt: CNN projects Democrats past 250 seats after Amish Shah's Arizona flip, with the AP count at 253 and at least 30 Republican incumbents beaten.
body:
• Democrats have cleared 250 House seats, CNN projects, after Amish Shah's flip in Arizona's 1st District delivered the party's 40th pickup of the cycle.
  • The Associated Press had called 253 races for Democrats and 155 for Republicans by Thursday afternoon, with 27 races still undecided — already the party's biggest House majority since its 257 seats in 2008.
  • At least 30 Republican incumbents have lost, including former Intelligence Committee chair Mike Turner and NRCC chair Richard Hudson, while Republicans flipped only one seat untouched by mid-decade redistricting.
  • For Indian-American readers, the scale matters: a majority this large lets Democratic leaders pass bills and open investigations even with defections, and Shah's Arizona win is part of a strong cycle for Indian-American candidates.

Democrats have passed 250 seats in the House of Representatives, CNN projected on Thursday, turning Tuesday's midterm vote into the party's biggest House victory since 2008. The milestone seat came in Arizona's 1st District, where Democrat Amish Shah flipped a Republican-held seat — the party's 40th pickup of the cycle, according to CNN reporting carried by World Pulse Wire.

The count is still moving. By Thursday afternoon, the Associated Press had called 253 races for Democrats and 155 for Republicans, with 27 races still to be decided, according to the New York Post figures cited in the same reporting. Newsmax, also citing the AP, projected Democrats will finish with at least 252 seats and noted the party had already flipped 38 seats.

Incumbents fell across the map

At least 30 Republican incumbents have been ousted, CNN reported, with losses spread from swing districts to seats Republicans had held for decades. In Virginia's 1st District, Shannon Taylor unseated Rob Wittman, who had held the seat since 2007. In Ohio, former House Intelligence Committee chairman Mike Turner, first elected in 2002, lost to Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker, the AP projected.

The defeats reached the Republican campaign leadership itself. Richard Hudson of North Carolina, who chairs the National Republican Congressional Committee, lost to Richard Ojeda and conceded on Wednesday, according to Newsmax. Republicans Juan Ciscomani of Arizona and Jeff Crank of Colorado were also defeated. Against that, the GOP flipped only one seat in a district unaffected by mid-decade redistricting — Maine's 2nd District — and Democrats retained at least 11 of the 15 Democratic-held districts Republicans had targeted. In North Carolina, Democrats could yet win 10 of the state's 14 seats despite a map drawn to favour Republicans in 11 of them. Live tallies are on the Associated Press election results page.

"A Watergate-level repudiation."

— Sen. Ted Cruz, on the Republican losses, via Newsmax

How the numbers compare

A majority above 250 seats is the largest either party has held since Democrats won 257 seats in 2008 alongside Barack Obama's first presidential victory, and it already exceeds any Republican majority since the Great Depression — the GOP high point in that span was 247 seats after the 2014 election. Democrats have won or lead in 259 districts; if those leads hold, the final total could reach 260, which would be the party's biggest majority since the 1991–93 Congress. Cook Political Report House editor Erin Covey told NPR that Democrats could finish with as many as 258 or 259 seats, surpassing the 2008 mark.

The size of the majority changes what the new Congress can do. With a cushion of more than 30 seats above the 218 needed for control, Democratic leaders can lose votes from their own side and still pass legislation, and the party takes the chairmanship of every House committee in January — with the subpoena and oversight powers that brings, as our election-night report on the Democratic sweep and Indian-American winners detailed.

What happens next

Counting continues in the remaining races, with votes still being tallied in Maine, Montana, Florida and Alaska, among other states, and two Senate contests — in Alaska and Mississippi — also uncalled. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries has said his party will finish with at least 255 seats. The new Congress convenes in January, when Democrats take the Speaker's gavel; before then, the outgoing Republican-led House must still pass government funding in a lame-duck session expected to be tense after the scale of the defeat.
